title: Mission: loan calculator with tests
subtitle: The canteen is financing a juice machine, and the first version of the code gets almost everything wrong
mission: Dona Cida is buying a R$ 1,000 juice machine and wants to know the installments: 12x at 2% a month, or 3x and 4x interest-free. An intern wrote Calculadora.Parcelas(valor, taxaMensalPct, meses) (Calculator.Installments(amount, monthlyRatePct, months)) with everything this track taught you to avoid: money in double, the rate divided as an integer, nothing for a zero rate, loose cents, no validation, a catch that swallows everything and a single test. Fix it until all six criteria turn green.

coach.ui: Move the controls; the criteria change as you adjust. Each failing one says why.
coach.cmd: Edit the command and run it. Each failing criterion says why. Everything showed up in lessons 1, 5 and 6.

why.simples:
You did what a good team does with money: kept the values in the type that counts in base 10 (decimal), computed the rate without losing the fraction, thought about the odd case (with no interest, the formula would divide by zero), rounded to cents and made the last installment close the bill, refused nonsense input with a clear exception and wrote a test for each of those cases.
The tests are the part that stays: a year from now, when someone "improves" the calculator, they’ll tell you right away if the math went wrong again.
why.dev:
The formula is the standard amortized (Price) installment: payment = amount × i × (1 + i)^n / ((1 + i)^n − 1). Since Math.Pow only takes double, the decimal power is a loop of multiplications. With i = 0 the formula becomes 0 / 0: in double that silently gives NaN, in decimal it throws DivideByZeroException; that’s why the interest-free case has its own path (amount / months).
Round only at the end, with an explicit MidpointRounding (Math.Round’s default is banker’s rounding, ToEven), and leave the difference on the last installment: 1000 / 3 = 333.33 + 333.33 + 333.34. Validation throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException with the parameter’s nameof, and the xUnit tests cover the happy path, both zero-rate cases and invalid input with Assert.Throws.
why.especialista:
A real financial system still needs: the rounding rule defined by the business (and sometimes by regulation), the amortization schedule with the last installment computed from the outstanding balance, dates and business days, taxes and other charges, and the type of values at the edges (JSON and database: use numeric/decimal in the database and serialize as an exact number or a string, never as double).
Tests: beyond examples, property tests ("the installments never add up to more than amount × (1 + i)^n plus a few cents", "for i = 0 the sum is exactly the amount") catch cases nobody thought of; and a [Theory] with [InlineData] organizes the example table (attributes don’t accept decimal literals, so pass double or string and convert, or use [MemberData]). Validate public input with .NET’s guard helpers, like ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegativeOrZero (.NET 8 or newer).

success: Mission accomplished! {done} of 6 criteria: 12 installments of R$ 94.56, R$ 1,000 in 3 interest-free payments closing at 333.33 + 333.33 + 333.34, absurd input refused with ArgumentOutOfRangeException and {passN} green tests to prove all of it. The juice machine can come in now.

controls.zeroRate: Own path for a zero rate
controls.cents: Round to cents and close the bill

steps:
In an empty folder, create the library and the test project and link them:
dotnet new classlib -o Emprestimo
dotnet new xunit -o Emprestimo.Tests
dotnet add Emprestimo.Tests reference Emprestimo
Delete Emprestimo/Class1.cs and Emprestimo.Tests/UnitTest1.cs.
Run the tests: cd Emprestimo.Tests and then dotnet test (the first run downloads the NuGet packages).
Break it on purpose: in Calculadora.cs, change the first if (taxa == 0) to if (false) and run dotnet test again (the compiler warns about unreachable code, and that’s fine).
recipe.ok: dotnet test ends with 4 tests passed and no failures; with the if (false), the zero-rate and cents tests fail with DivideByZeroException and the other two still pass.
